addmaths-0606-circles-equations-of-circl.description: Translate between the geometry and both common equation forms.

sections.title: Where are the centre and radius in the equation?
sections.label: Expanded
sections.intro: The distance from a point on the boundary to the centre is fixed. Squaring the distance gives the equation.

blocks.html: Centre \((a,b)\) and radius \(r\) give \((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2\). Complete both squares when the equation has been expanded.

figure.alt: Circle with centre C and a radius to P
figure.caption: Every point on the circumference has the same distance from C.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has the equation \(x^2+y^2+16x-6y-96=0\).

Give the coordinates of its centre.
blocks.hint: Complete both squares and read the centre.
blocks.solution:
Complete the square separately in x and y to get \((x+8)^2+(y-3)^2=169\).

Read each coordinate with the sign opposite to the constant in its bracket.

\((-8,3)\)

blocks.html: When a bracket contains a plus sign, its corresponding centre coordinate is negative.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has the equation \(x^2+y^2+12x-6y-124=0\).

Give the coordinates of its centre.
blocks.hint: Complete both squares and read the centre.
blocks.solution:
Complete the square separately in x and y to get \((x+6)^2+(y-3)^2=169\).

Read each coordinate with the sign opposite to the constant in its bracket.

\((-6,3)\)

blocks.html: Add both completing-square corrections to the other side of the original equation as well.

sections.title: How can a diameter tell me the centre?
sections.label: Diameter
sections.intro: The centre lies halfway between the two ends. Use the midpoint first, then find the distance from there to either end.

blocks.html: A radius is half the diameter. The squared radius can be obtained from the squared coordinate differences from centre to endpoint.

figure.alt: A segment from P to Q passes through C at the midpoint. P and Q lie on the circle.
figure.caption: Find the midpoint first. The radius is the distance from that midpoint to either endpoint.

blocks.prompt:
The points \(P(11,-7)\) and \(Q(1,17)\) are the ends of a circle's diameter.

Find the centre.
blocks.hint: Use the midpoint of the diameter.
blocks.solution:
Average the x-coordinates of the endpoints and average their y-coordinates.

\((6,5)\)

blocks.html: The distance between the two given endpoints is the whole diameter.

blocks.prompt:
The points \(P(13,-7)\) and \(Q(3,17)\) are the ends of a circle's diameter.

Find the centre.
blocks.hint: Use the midpoint of the diameter.
blocks.solution:
Average the x-coordinates of the endpoints and average their y-coordinates.

\((8,5)\)

blocks.html: Substitute both endpoints into your final equation to check.

sections.title: How do I use a point on the circle?
sections.label: Boundary
sections.intro: Subtract matched coordinates from centre to point. Pythagoras uses these signed changes after squaring.

blocks.html: The squared distance from the centre to any boundary point is the constant in centre–radius form.

blocks.prompt:
A circle with centre \(C(1,8)\) passes through \(P(6,-4)\).

Find its radius.
blocks.hint: Use the centre-to-boundary distance.
blocks.solution:
The displacement from centre to boundary has components \(5\) and \(-12\). Use Pythagoras for its length.

\(13\)

blocks.html: Expanding a squared bracket also creates a linear term.

blocks.prompt:
A circle with centre \(C(3,8)\) passes through \(P(8,-4)\).

Find its radius.
blocks.hint: Use the centre-to-boundary distance.
blocks.solution:
The displacement from centre to boundary has components \(5\) and \(-12\). Use Pythagoras for its length.

\(13\)

blocks.html: Keep the radius squared in your calculations if the question only needs an equation.

examples.title: The centre hidden in an expanded circle
examples.question:
A circle has the equation \(x^2+y^2-20x-4y-65=0\).

  1. Give the coordinates of its centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the radius.

    [2]

  3. Write the equation in centre–radius form.

    [2]
solution: (a) Complete the square separately in x and y to get \((x-10)^2+(y-2)^2=169\).
Read each coordinate with the sign opposite to the constant in its bracket.
(b) Completing the squares gives \((x-10)^2+(y-2)^2=169\). The positive square root of \(169\) is \(13\).
(c) The centre is \((10,2)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).

examples.title: The centre hidden in an expanded circle
examples.question:
A circle has the equation \(x^2+y^2+6x-6y-151=0\).

  1. Give the coordinates of its centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the radius.

    [2]

  3. Write the equation in centre–radius form.

    [2]
solution: (a) Complete the square separately in x and y to get \((x+3)^2+(y-3)^2=169\).
Read each coordinate with the sign opposite to the constant in its bracket.
(b) Completing the squares gives \((x+3)^2+(y-3)^2=169\). The positive square root of \(169\) is \(13\).
(c) The centre is \((-3,3)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).

examples.title: Find a circle from the ends of its diameter
examples.question:
The points \(P(10,-7)\) and \(Q(0,17)\) are the ends of a circle's diameter.

  1. Find the centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the squared radius.

    [2]

  3. Write the equation in centre–radius form.

    [2]
solution: (a) Average the x-coordinates of the endpoints and average their y-coordinates.
(b) From \((5,5)\) to \((10,-7)\), the coordinate changes are \(5\) and \(-12\).
Add their squares to get \(169\).
(c) The centre is \((5,5)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).

examples.title: Find a circle from the ends of its diameter
examples.question:

    [2]

    [2]
solution: (a) Average the x-coordinates of the endpoints and average their y-coordinates.
(b) From \((-8,6)\) to \((-3,-6)\), the coordinate changes are \(5\) and \(-12\).
Add their squares to get \(169\).
(c) The centre is \((-8,6)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).

examples.title: From a centre and a boundary point
examples.question:
A circle with centre \(C(0,8)\) passes through \(P(5,-4)\).

  1. Find its radius.

    [2]

  2. Write the equation in centre–radius form.

    [2]

  3. Write the equation in expanded form.

    [2]
solution: (a) The displacement from centre to boundary has components \(5\) and \(-12\). Use Pythagoras for its length.
(b) The centre is \((0,8)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).
(c) Expand both squared brackets in \(x^2+(y-8)^2=169\), then bring the constant to the left.

(b) The centre is \((6,8)\) and the squared radius is \(169\).
(c) Expand both squared brackets in \((x-6)^2+(y-8)^2=169\), then bring the constant to the left.

addmaths-0606-circles-intersections-with.description: Solve for both coordinates and interpret the number of intersections.

sections.title: How does a horizontal line simplify the circle equation?
sections.label: Horizontal
sections.intro: Every point on a horizontal line has the same y-value. Substituting it leaves an equation in x.

blocks.html: A positive squared difference gives two x-values. Use the fixed y-coordinate to form both complete coordinate pairs.

figure.alt: A circle cut by a horizontal line at P and Q
figure.caption: Substitute the same y-value to find both x-values.

blocks.prompt:
A circle is given by \((x-5)^2+(y-3)^2=25\). A line has equation \(y=6\).

Find both points where the line crosses the circle.
blocks.hint: Substitute the line equation into the circle and solve both branches.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the given y-value. This gives \((x-5)^2=16\).

The signed difference \(x-5\) can be \(4\) or \(-4\).

\((1,6),\ (9,6)\)

blocks.html: Taking only the positive square root usually loses one intersection.

blocks.prompt:
A circle is given by \((x-7)^2+(y-3)^2=25\). A line has equation \(y=6\).

Find both points where the line crosses the circle.
blocks.hint: Substitute the line equation into the circle and solve both branches.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the given y-value. This gives \((x-7)^2=16\).

The signed difference \(x-7\) can be \(4\) or \(-4\).

\((3,6),\ (11,6)\)

blocks.html: Check whether both candidate points also satisfy the given line equation.

sections.title: How do I substitute a sloping line?
sections.label: Diagonal
sections.intro: Replace y with its expression from the line. Then solve the resulting quadratic before finding y separately for each root.

blocks.html: Substitution preserves points shared by both equations. A line through the centre cuts a diameter.

blocks.prompt:
The line \(y=x+6\) meets the circle \(x^2+(y-6)^2=2\) in two points.

Find both points of intersection.
blocks.hint: Substitute the line expression into the two squared distances.
blocks.solution:
From the line equation, \(y-6=x\).

Substitute to get \(2(x)^2=2\). Solve with both signs and recover y from the line.

\((-1,5),\ (1,7)\)

blocks.html: Two roots for x need two corresponding y-values.

blocks.prompt:
The line \(y=x+4\) meets the circle \((x-2)^2+(y-6)^2=2\) in two points.

Find both points of intersection.
blocks.hint: Substitute the line expression into the two squared distances.
blocks.solution:
From the line equation, \(y-6=x-2\).

Substitute to get \(2(x-2)^2=2\). Solve with both signs and recover y from the line.

\((1,5),\ (3,7)\)

blocks.html: Rearrange for the variable that makes the substitution shortest.

sections.title: How can I tell whether a line is a tangent?
sections.label: Count
sections.intro: Study the number of roots after substitution. A line and circle may share two points, one point or no point.

blocks.html: A tangent has one distinct point in common with the circle. A non-vertical line can be tested by the discriminant of the substituted quadratic.

figure.alt: A solid vertical line L intersects a circle twice. The two dashed vertical tangents touch the circle once each.
figure.caption: Compare the horizontal distance from the centre to each vertical line with the radius.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(L\) be the line \(x=-3\) and let \(C\) be the circle \((x+5)^2+(y-9)^2=9\).

How many distinct points do the line and circle share?
blocks.hint: Classify the substituted equation by the sign of its right-hand side.
blocks.solution:
Substitute into the circle to get \((y-9)^2=5\).

A positive right-hand side gives two roots, zero gives one and a negative value gives none.

2 points.

blocks.html: A repeated root counts as one coordinate value.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(L\) be the line \(x=-1\) and let \(C\) be the circle \((x+3)^2+(y-9)^2=9\).

How many distinct points do the line and circle share?
blocks.hint: Classify the substituted equation by the sign of its right-hand side.
blocks.solution:
Substitute into the circle to get \((y-9)^2=5\).

A positive right-hand side gives two roots, zero gives one and a negative value gives none.

2 points.

blocks.html: For a vertical line, substitute its fixed x-value directly.

examples.title: The two ends of a horizontal chord
examples.question:
A circle is given by \((x-4)^2+(y-3)^2=25\). A line has equation \(y=6\).

  1. Find both points where the line crosses the circle.

    [2]

  2. Find the chord length.

    [2]

  3. Find the distance from the centre to the line.

    [2]
solution: (a) Substitute the given y-value. This gives \((x-4)^2=16\).
The signed difference \(x-4\) can be \(4\) or \(-4\).
(b) The chord is horizontal, so subtract the smaller x-coordinate from the larger one.
(c) The perpendicular to a horizontal line is vertical. Use the change between \(3\) and \(6\).

(b) The chord is horizontal, so subtract the smaller x-coordinate from the larger one.
(c) The perpendicular to a horizontal line is vertical. Use the change between \(3\) and \(6\).

examples.title: A diagonal through the centre
examples.question:
The line \(y=x+7\) meets the circle \((x+1)^2+(y-6)^2=2\) in two points.

  1. Find both points of intersection.

    [2]

  2. Find the midpoint of the chord.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the chord is a diameter.

    [1]
solution: (a) From the line equation, \(y-6=x+1\).
Substitute to get \(2(x+1)^2=2\). Solve with both signs and recover y from the line.
(b) The two intersections have equal and opposite displacements from the centre.
(c) The circle's centre lies on the line segment between its two boundary points.
It passes through the centre of the circle.

(b) The two intersections have equal and opposite displacements from the centre.
(c) The circle's centre lies on the line segment between its two boundary points.
It passes through the centre of the circle.

examples.title: Does a vertical line meet the circle?
examples.question:
Let \(L\) be the line \(x=-4\) and let \(C\) be the circle \((x+6)^2+(y-9)^2=9\).

  1. How many distinct points do the line and circle share?

    [2]

  2. Give the equations of both vertical lines tangent to \(C\).

    [2]
solution: (a) Substitute into the circle to get \((y-9)^2=5\).
A positive right-hand side gives two roots, zero gives one and a negative value gives none.
2 points.
(b) Each tangent is horizontally \(3\) units from the centre.

A positive right-hand side gives two roots, zero gives one and a negative value gives none.

(b) Each tangent is horizontally \(3\) units from the centre.

addmaths-0606-circles-equations-of-tange.description: Use the radius direction and point of contact to write a tangent equation.

sections.title: Which gradient belongs to the tangent?
sections.label: Negative reciprocal
sections.intro: Mark the centre and point of contact. The radius between them is perpendicular to the tangent.

blocks.html: For finite nonzero radius gradient \(m_r\), the tangent gradient is \(-\frac{1}{m_r}\).

figure.alt: A tangent perpendicular to the radius at P
figure.caption: At P the tangent has a right angle with the radius.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x+1)^2+(y-4)^2=25\). The point \(P(2,8)\) lies on the circle.

Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal and the point of contact.
blocks.solution:
The radius from \((-1,4)\) to \((2,8)\) has gradient \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The tangent has gradient \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=\frac{19}{2}\).

\(y=-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{19}{2}\)

blocks.html: The radius gradient is the one you need to convert. Using it directly gives a line through the circle.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x-1)^2+(y-4)^2=25\). The point \(P(4,8)\) lies on the circle.

Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal and the point of contact.
blocks.solution:
The radius from \((1,4)\) to \((4,8)\) has gradient \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The tangent has gradient \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=11\).

\(y=-\frac{3}{4}x+11\)

blocks.html: Put the point of contact back into your tangent equation.

sections.title: What if a radius is horizontal or vertical?
sections.label: Axis tangents
sections.intro: Use direction rather than a reciprocal when a gradient is zero or undefined.

blocks.html: A vertical radius gives a tangent \(y=k\). A horizontal radius gives a tangent \(x=h\).

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x+6)^2+(y-7)^2=4\) and is tangent to a line at \(P(-6,5)\).

Find the equation of the tangent.
blocks.hint: Use the perpendicular radius direction.
blocks.solution:
The centre is \((-6,7)\). The radius to \(P\) is vertical, so the tangent is horizontal.

\(y=5\)

blocks.html: A vertical tangent cannot be written as y = mx + c.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x+4)^2+(y-7)^2=4\) and is tangent to a line at \(P(-4,5)\).

Find the equation of the tangent.
blocks.hint: Use the perpendicular radius direction.
blocks.solution:
The centre is \((-4,7)\). The radius to \(P\) is vertical, so the tangent is horizontal.

\(y=5\)

blocks.html: Read h or k from the point of contact.

sections.title: Where is a second parallel tangent?
sections.label: Parallel
sections.intro: All radii to parallel tangents have the same line direction. Their contact points lie at opposite ends of a diameter.

blocks.html: Reflect the first contact point in the centre. Use the same tangent gradient and the reflected point to find the new intercept.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x-8)^2+(y-9)^2=25\). The point \(P(11,5)\) lies on the circle.

Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal and the point of contact.
blocks.solution:
The radius from \((8,9)\) to \((11,5)\) has gradient \(-\frac{4}{3}\).

The tangent has gradient \(\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=-\frac{13}{4}\).

\(y=\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{13}{4}\)

blocks.html: The intercept is usually different on the two tangents.

blocks.prompt:
A circle has equation \((x-10)^2+(y-9)^2=25\). The point \(P(13,5)\) lies on the circle.

Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal and the point of contact.
blocks.solution:
The radius from \((10,9)\) to \((13,5)\) has gradient \(-\frac{4}{3}\).

The tangent has gradient \(\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=-\frac{19}{4}\).

\(y=\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{19}{4}\)

blocks.html: Find the other contact point before writing the line.

examples.title: The tangent perpendicular to a sloping radius
examples.question:
A circle has equation \((x+2)^2+(y-4)^2=25\). The point \(P(1,8)\) lies on the circle.

  1. Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the y-intercept of the tangent.

    [2]
solution: (a) The radius from \((-2,4)\) to \((1,8)\) has gradient \(\frac{4}{3}\).
The tangent has gradient \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=\frac{35}{4}\).

examples.title: The tangent perpendicular to a sloping radius
examples.question:
A circle has equation \((x-4)^2+(y-4)^2=25\). The point \(P(7,8)\) lies on the circle.

  1. Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the y-intercept of the tangent.

    [2]
solution: (a) The radius from \((4,4)\) to \((7,8)\) has gradient \(\frac{4}{3}\).
The tangent has gradient \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Substitute the point of contact into \(y=mx+c\) to get \(c=\frac{53}{4}\).
(b) Use \(x=0\) in \(y=-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{53}{4}\) to obtain \(y=\frac{53}{4}\).

examples.title: Tangent at the end of a vertical radius
examples.question:
A circle has equation \((x+7)^2+(y-7)^2=4\) and is tangent to a line at \(P(-7,5)\).

  1. Find the equation of the tangent.

    [2]

  2. Find the point of contact of the parallel tangent.

    [2]

  3. Give the distance between the parallel tangents.

    [2]
solution: (a) The centre is \((-7,7)\). The radius to \(P\) is vertical, so the tangent is horizontal.
(b) The second point lies the same distance \(2\) from the centre on the opposite side.
(c) The vertical separation is the diameter of the circle.

examples.title: Two parallel tangents to a circle

A circle has equation \((x-7)^2+(y-9)^2=25\). The point \(P(10,13)\) lies on the circle.

  1. Find the equation of the tangent at \(P\).

    [3]

  2. Find the contact point of the other tangent parallel to it.

    [2]

  3. Find the equation of the other tangent.

    [2]
solution: (a) The radius from \((7,9)\) to \((10,13)\) has gradient \(\frac{4}{3}\).

glossary.definition: The only point shared by a tangent and its circle.

revision.body:
Which gradient belongs to the tangent?

For finite nonzero radius gradient \(m_r\), the tangent gradient is \(-\frac{1}{m_r}\).

What if a radius is horizontal or vertical?

A vertical radius gives a tangent \(y=k\). A horizontal radius gives a tangent \(x=h\).

Where is a second parallel tangent?

Reflect the first contact point in the centre. Use the same tangent gradient and the reflected point to find the new intercept.

addmaths-0606-circles-two-circles.description: Classify how two circles meet and calculate the common line and points.

sections.title: What does the distance between the centres tell me?
sections.label: Centre distance
sections.intro: Find both radii and the distance between the centres. Compare the distance to the radius sum and their positive difference.

blocks.html: Two distinct circles meet twice when \(|r_1-r_2|0\). For external touching, \(d=r_1+r_2\).

blocks.prompt:
Circle \(C_1\) has equation \((x+7)^2+(y-5)^2=9\) and circle \(C_2\) has equation \((x-2)^2+(y-5)^2=25\).

How are the circles positioned?

options.B: One circle lies inside the other, without touching
options.C: Disjoint, neither circle inside the other

blocks.hint: Compare the centre distance to the sum and difference of the radii.
blocks.solution:
The centre separation is \(9\). The radii are \(3\) and \(5\).

The radius difference is \(2\) and the sum is \(8\). Compare both bounds to classify the circles.

Disjoint, neither circle inside the other.

blocks.html: A centre distance below the radius difference means strict containment. Coincident circles have the same centre and radius.

blocks.prompt:

options.D: One circle lies inside the other, without touching

blocks.hint: Compare the centre distance to the sum and difference of the radii.
blocks.solution:

The radius difference is \(2\) and the sum is \(8\). Compare both bounds to classify the circles.

Disjoint, neither circle inside the other.

blocks.html: Compute both bounds before deciding the type of intersection.

sections.title: Why does subtracting two circle equations produce a line?
sections.label: Chord
sections.intro: A common point satisfies both circle equations at once. Their expanded squared terms have equal coefficients.

blocks.html: Subtract to cancel the squares. For intersecting circles the resulting linear equation gives the line containing the chord.

figure.alt: Two intersecting circles with a vertical common chord
figure.caption: The two intersections lie on a single straight line. Subtracting the circle equations gives that line.

blocks.prompt:
The circles \((x-7)^2+(y-7)^2=25\) and \((x-13)^2+(y-7)^2=25\) have two common points.

Find the equation of the line through the two common points.
blocks.hint: Subtract the two equations and solve the resulting linear relation.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the circle equations. The squared terms cancel and the difference gives \(12x=120\).

The line through both points therefore has constant x-coordinate \(10\).

\(x=10\)

blocks.html: The linear equation contains points outside the circles too.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Subtract the two equations and solve the resulting linear relation.
blocks.solution:

The line through both points therefore has constant x-coordinate \(12\).

\(x=12\)

blocks.html: After finding the chord line, substitute it into a circle to find the actual common points.

sections.title: What changes when the radii are different?
sections.label: Unequal
sections.intro: For equal radii the common chord is halfway between the centres. With unequal radii its position needs the actual equations.

blocks.html: Subtract the full equations, including their constants and squared radii. Check the resulting points in both originals.

blocks.hint: Subtract the two equations and solve the resulting linear relation.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the circle equations. The squared terms cancel and the difference gives \(28x=196\).

The line through both points therefore has constant x-coordinate \(7\).

\(x=7\)

blocks.html: The midpoint of the centre segment does not generally lie on the common chord.

examples.title: Using radii and centre distance
examples.question:
Circle \(C_1\) has equation \((x+8)^2+(y-5)^2=9\) and circle \(C_2\) has equation \(x^2+(y-5)^2=25\).

  1. How are the circles positioned?

    [2]

  2. How many points do their circumferences have in common?

    [1]
solution: (a) The centre separation is \(8\). The radii are \(3\) and \(5\).
The radius difference is \(2\) and the sum is \(8\). Compare both bounds to classify the circles.
Touch externally.
(b) Equality with one of the bounds gives one point. Strict containment or strict separation gives none.

examples.title: The line of a common chord
examples.question:
The circles \((x-6)^2+(y-7)^2=25\) and \((x-12)^2+(y-7)^2=25\) have two common points.

  1. Find the equation of the line through the two common points.

    [2]

  2. Find both common points.

    [2]

  3. Find the chord length.

    [2]
solution: (a) Subtract the circle equations. The squared terms cancel and the difference gives \(12x=108\).
The line through both points therefore has constant x-coordinate \(9\).
(b) Substitute \(x=9\) into the first equation to obtain \((y-7)^2=16\).
Use both signs, then check the second circle equation.
(c) The chord is vertical and the y-values are \(3\) and \(11\).
